ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: On the left side of the figure is a substituent represented by R connected to an alkynyl group, and the right-end alkyne carbon is connected to Br; overall it can be read as R–C≡C–Br. In the figure there is a curved arrow from negatively charged Bu− pointing toward Br, and another curved arrow indicates that the electron pair of the C–Br bond transfers to the side of the terminal carbon of the alkynyl group. Reasoning: Pushing electrons according to the arrows, Bu− attacks Br, while the C–Br bond breaks, and the bond electrons remain on the terminal alkyne carbon connected to Br. Therefore the organic skeleton becomes R–C≡C−. When represented with SMILES, the R substituent is represented by [*], and the negatively charged terminal alkyne carbon is written as [C-], so the product state is [*]C#[C-].

raw_record.question_text: An 'arrow-pushing' diagram is a common type of chemical image used to illustrate electron flow in mechanistic steps. Please choose the SMILES expression for the molecules(state) after the electron has been relocated, as depicted in the image. <image_1>

method.method_draft: Identify the substrate in the image as R–C≡C–Br. Apply the arrows: Bu− attacks Br, and the C–Br bond breaks with the electron pair ending on the terminal alkyne carbon. The remaining carbon skeleton is R–C≡C⁻. Encode R as [*] and the negatively charged terminal carbon as [C-], giving [*]C#[C-].

planner_metadata.image_role: Read the image as an R-substituted bromoalkyne, R–C≡C–Br. Note the curved arrow from the butyl anion toward Br and the curved arrow showing the C–Br bonding electrons moving back onto the alkyne carbon formerly bonded to Br.
planner_metadata.text_role: Use the prompt instruction that the answer should be the SMILES expression for the molecular state after the depicted electron relocation.
planner_metadata.knowledge_role: In arrow-pushing notation, electrons move from the tail to the arrowhead. If the C–Br bond electrons are assigned to carbon while Br is captured by Bu−, the carbon loses its bond to Br and gains a lone pair/negative charge. The generic R group is represented in SMILES as [*].

method.method_draft: Treat the pictured step as transfer/removal of Br from R–C≡C–Br by Bu−. After Br is removed, preserve the alkyne C≡C skeleton and assign the residual negative charge to the terminal carbon that had been bonded to Br. The product fragment is R–C≡C⁻, which is written in SMILES as [*]C#[C-].

planner_metadata.distinctiveness_rationale: Uses formal charge and bromine-transfer bookkeeping rather than step-by-step arrow tracing; it infers the same intermediate from conservation of bonds and charge.
planner_metadata.image_role: Read the image as showing a bromoalkyne with a generic left substituent R and a bromine on the right alkyne carbon, plus Bu− positioned to interact with Br.
planner_metadata.text_role: Use the question only to know that the requested output is the post-electron-relocation SMILES, not a mechanistic explanation.
planner_metadata.knowledge_role: When a nucleophile donates to a halogen in this kind of halogen-transfer/dehalogenation depiction, Br is removed from the carbon framework. Charge conservation then places the negative charge on the carbon that lost Br, because that carbon retains the former C–Br electron pair while the C≡C bond remains intact. The R placeholder maps to [*] in SMILES.
